Attention-deficit disorder is usually described as a deficit of attention, but Gabor Maté argues that the label conceals more than it explains (Maté, 1999). In *Scattered Minds* he proposes that the characteristic distractibility is better understood as a developmental adaptation: a nervous system that learned, early and under stress, to tune out what it could not bear to tune in [1]. This reframing matters because it moves the question from what is wrong with the child to what happened in the child's environment.

## The Biology of Attention

Maté grounds the argument in the neurobiology of the prefrontal cortex, which regulates attention and impulse and which develops largely after birth [2]. Its circuits are shaped by the emotional attunement of caregivers, and chronic stress in the caregiving environment can impair their development (Schore, 1994). On this account, the behaviour that teachers read as defiance or laziness is the visible output of a regulatory system that never received the conditions it needed.

The claim is not that parents cause the disorder. Maté is careful to say that heredity confers a sensitivity, and that the environment determines how that sensitivity is expressed [3]. The distinction is important, because it removes blame without removing responsibility.

## What Follows From This

If the disorder is an adaptation, then medication can be useful but cannot be sufficient. The deeper work is to create, in adulthood, the relational conditions that were missing in childhood: patience, acceptance, and the experience of being attuned to [4]. Maté describes this as a process of self-parenting, and he is explicit that it is slow work that unfolds over years rather than weeks.

The reframing does not make the problem smaller. It makes it more human, and it suggests that the most effective interventions will be the ones that treat the person as a whole rather than as a set of symptoms to be managed.
